lines: A plan that reruns on a schedule still has to decide what it's allowed to forget.
Here's the rule that draws that line, and bounds how much the engine has to keep around.
Here's that rule, built by hand from the data itself.
Take the latest time the engine has ever seen, back off by the delay configured, and that's the exact number Spark reports back, one trigger behind.
Here's a case worth thinking through before the answer comes.
An event shows up after its own moment has passed, but still inside that delay. Does the engine take it in, or has it already moved on?
steps.answer: Taken in. The slot it belongs to hasn't closed yet, even though the event itself is late.

lines: Taken in, correctly.
Late against the newest thing seen, yes, but the slot that event belongs to is still open for business.
So lateness by itself was never the deciding factor.
What actually decides is whether the slot that event belongs to is still open, or has already been closed out for good.
Here's the harder version of the same question.
Send that identical lateness in again, only one round later, after the cutoff has moved past where that slot ends. Taken, or refused this time?
steps.answer: Refused completely. Nothing about the event changed; the cutoff moved past it instead.

lines: Refused, completely, this time.
Nothing changed about the event between the two attempts. What moved was the cutoff, past the far edge of the slot that would have held it.
So a slot doesn't fade out gradually.
It closes the instant the cutoff passes its own far edge, and there's no partial credit for almost making it in time.
Feed this from several sources at once, and there's a choice to make.
Hold everyone to the slowest source's own pace, or let the fastest one set it and give up some of the slower one's own data.
One number, built from the newest time seen, minus a delay.
One real cost that comes with it: the engine forgets a slot the moment that number crosses its edge, no matter how close the data came.
